p: My name is Tom. I am sixteen. I live in a small flat with my mum and my sister, Anna.
I get up at seven o'clock. First, I drink a glass of water. Then I do ten push-ups. After that, I have a shower.
For breakfast I eat eggs and bread. Anna eats porridge. Mum drinks coffee, but I drink tea.
At half past seven I take the bus to school. The bus is often late, so I read a book on the way. I like books about space.
q: Что Том делает первым делом утром?

p: We have a cat. Her name is Pepper. She is black with white feet. She is four years old.
Pepper sleeps a lot. In the morning she sleeps on my bed. In the afternoon she sleeps in a box near the window. She loves the sun.
Pepper doesn't like dogs, and she doesn't like rain. When it rains, she sits under the table and looks angry.
Every evening my dad gives her fish. Then she is very happy, and she plays with a small red ball.

p: On Saturday I don't go to school. I wake up at nine. The weather is nice: it is sunny and warm.
I call my friend Max. We go to the park by bike. In the park there are many people. Some people run, some people walk with their dogs.
Max and I play football for one hour. Then we are hungry, so we buy two ice creams. My ice cream is chocolate, and Max's ice cream is strawberry.

p: Lisa goes to the shop after work. She needs milk, apples and bread.
The shop is small, but it has everything. Lisa takes a basket. She finds the milk and the bread quickly. But there are no green apples today, only red apples. Lisa takes six red apples.
At the till, the woman says, "That's five pounds, please." Lisa gives her a ten-pound note. The woman gives her five pounds back and says, "Have a nice evening!"
Lisa walks home. It is cold, and she wants a cup of hot tea.

p: My grandfather is seventy years old, but he is very active. He lives in a village near a big lake.
Every day he walks five kilometres. In summer he swims in the lake. In winter he goes skiing. He says, "Moving is good for the body and for the head."
He has a garden with potatoes, carrots and tomatoes. I visit him every August. We work in the garden in the morning, and in the evening we play chess. He always wins!

t: The First Day at the Gym
p: Last Monday Kate went to the gym for the first time. She was nervous. She thought that everyone there was strong and fit, and that people would look at her.

When she arrived, a young trainer called Sam met her at the door. He showed her the machines and explained how to use them. "Don't try to do everything today," he said. "Start with fifteen minutes on the bike and some easy exercises. The most important thing is to come back on Wednesday."

Kate was surprised. Nobody looked at her. An old man was walking slowly on a running machine, two girls were talking and laughing, and a big man was reading something on his phone between exercises. Everyone was busy with their own workout.

After twenty-five minutes Kate felt tired but proud. She wrote in her notebook: "Day 1 — done." On Wednesday she came back, and on Friday too. Now, after two months, she goes three times a week. She still isn't very strong, but she isn't nervous any more.

p: Dear Mark,
I'm writing to you from Madrid! I arrived here three weeks ago for a language course, and I'm living with a Spanish family. They have two children, a dog and a very old piano that nobody plays.

The course is hard but interesting. We have lessons from nine to one every day. Our teacher, Carmen, never speaks English to us, only Spanish. At first I understood almost nothing, but now I can understand about half of what she says.
In the afternoons I walk around the city. My favourite place is a big park with a lake where people row small boats. Yesterday I tried it for the first time and nearly fell into the water!
The food is great, but people here eat dinner very late, at about ten o'clock. I'm always hungry by eight.
At the weekends the family takes me to small towns near Madrid. Last Saturday we visited a town with an old castle on a hill.
I'll be back in July. Let's meet and I'll show you my photos.

p: Last month my teacher gave our class a strange task: spend one week without a smartphone. We could use a normal phone for calls, but no social media, no games and no videos. Most of my classmates said it was impossible.

The first two days were really difficult. I kept putting my hand in my pocket to check the phone, but it wasn't there. At the bus stop I didn't know what to do with my eyes. I felt bored and a little lonely.

On the third day something changed. I started to notice things: a new café on my street, the old woman who feeds birds every morning, the funny names of shops. In the evenings I had much more time. I finished a book that I had started in September, and I helped my dad repair his bike.
The biggest surprise was sleep. Without videos in bed, I fell asleep about an hour earlier, and I woke up less tired.
When the week ended, I didn't stop using my phone. But now I leave it in the kitchen at night, and I don't take it out at the bus stop.

p: Every Sunday my grandmother makes pancakes, and last Sunday she finally taught me her recipe. "It's very easy," she said. "The secret is not the recipe. The secret is patience."

First, we mixed two eggs with a spoon of sugar and a little salt. Then we added half a litre of warm milk and slowly put in the flour, about two cups. Grandma told me to mix carefully, so there were no lumps. At the end we added two spoons of oil.
"Now wait," she said. "The mixture must rest for twenty minutes." I didn't understand why, but I waited.

The first pancake was a disaster. It stuck to the pan and broke into pieces. Grandma laughed and said that the first pancake is always bad, even for her. The pan has to get hot enough. The second pancake was better, and the third one was perfect: thin, golden and round.
We made twenty pancakes and ate them with honey and sour cream. Next Sunday I'm going to make them alone.

p: It was my second day in London. I wanted to go to the British Museum, so I took the number 24 bus. I sat by the window and looked at the beautiful old buildings. I was very happy.

After half an hour, I noticed that the buildings were not old and beautiful any more. There were small houses, gardens and a big supermarket. I was not in the centre of London. I was going the wrong way!
I got off the bus and asked a woman for help. She smiled and said that I needed the same bus, but in the other direction. "Don't worry," she said, "it happens to everybody."
I crossed the road and waited. Fifteen minutes later the bus came. When I finally arrived at the museum, it was almost closed. I had only forty minutes inside.
But I don't feel sad about that day. I saw a part of London that tourists usually don't see, and I learned an important lesson: always check the direction of the bus!

p: Two years ago I couldn't run to the end of my street. I was tired all the time, I slept badly, and I spent my evenings on the sofa with my phone. One day my younger brother asked me to play football with him, and after five minutes I had to stop. I felt ashamed.

That evening I found a simple plan on the internet. It was called "From the sofa to five kilometres" and it took nine weeks. In the first week you run for only one minute, then walk for ninety seconds, and repeat this eight times. It sounded too easy, but for me it was hard enough.

I ran three times a week, always early in the morning before work, because in the evening I always found excuses. Some days it rained, and I ran anyway. Some days my legs hurt, and I walked more than I ran.
In the ninth week I ran five kilometres without stopping for the first time. It took me thirty-four minutes. I wasn't fast, but I cried a little at the finish.
Now I run four times a week, and next spring I want to try a half marathon. And yes — now I can play football with my brother for the whole game.

p: When Maya turned eighteen, she decided to do something useful with her free time. She had always loved animals, but her flat was too small for a dog, and her landlord didn't allow pets. So she looked for volunteer work and found a small animal shelter on the edge of the city.

On her first Saturday she expected to play with puppies. Instead, she spent four hours cleaning cages, washing bowls and carrying heavy bags of food. By the end of the day her back hurt and her clothes smelled terrible. On the bus home she seriously thought about not coming back.

But something made her return. It was an old grey dog called Bruno. He had lived at the shelter for almost two years because most visitors wanted young, cute animals. Bruno was shy and didn't like loud noises, but when Maya sat quietly next to his cage, he came and put his head against her hand.

After that, Maya came every Saturday. The manager of the shelter, a calm woman named Ruth, taught her how to walk nervous dogs, how to notice if an animal was ill and how to talk to people who wanted to adopt a pet. Maya learned that the most important job was not playing with animals, but helping them become ready for a new home.
She started taking Bruno for long walks in the park next to the shelter. Slowly he became more confident. He stopped hiding when strangers came, and he even learned to sit and wait for his food.

Six months later, a retired teacher came to the shelter. She said she wanted a quiet dog, not a puppy. Ruth looked at Maya, and Maya brought Bruno. The woman and the dog looked at each other for a long time, and then Bruno slowly walked over and lay down at her feet.
When Bruno left, Maya cried on the bus home again — but this time for a completely different reason.

t: How I Finally Learned to Speak
p: I studied English at school for ten years. I knew all the grammar rules, I could fill in gaps in exercises, and I usually got good marks. But when I first travelled abroad and a waiter asked me a simple question, my mind went completely empty. I just smiled and pointed at the menu.

That moment made me think. Why could I pass tests but not have a conversation? The answer was simple: I had practised reading and writing, but almost never speaking. In class we spoke maybe two or three minutes each lesson, and always about prepared topics.

So I changed my method. First, I started talking to myself. While cooking or walking, I described what I was doing in English: "Now I'm cutting the onions. They're making me cry." It felt silly, but it helped me find words faster.

Second, I found a conversation partner online — a man from Canada who wanted to learn Russian. We talked twice a week for an hour: thirty minutes in English and thirty minutes in Russian. At first I was very nervous and made lots of mistakes. He never laughed at them; he just repeated the correct version naturally, and I tried to use it next time.

Third, I stopped watching films with Russian subtitles. I switched to English subtitles, and later to no subtitles at all. In the beginning I understood about a third of the dialogue, but my ears slowly got used to the speed and the accents.

The biggest change was in my attitude. I stopped trying to speak perfectly. I realised that people don't care much about my grammar mistakes — they care whether they can understand me. A simple sentence with a mistake is better than a perfect sentence that never comes out of my mouth.

After about eight months, I travelled abroad again. This time, when the waiter asked if I wanted anything else, I answered, made a small joke, and he laughed. It was a tiny conversation, but for me it felt like a big victory.

t: The Teenager Who Couldn't Wake Up
p: Every school morning in Ben's house sounded the same. His mother knocked on his door at seven, then again at ten past seven, and at twenty past she came in and opened the curtains. Ben, fifteen, groaned and pulled the blanket over his head. His parents thought he was lazy. Ben thought he was just tired. Both were partly wrong.

Scientists have found that during the teenage years the body clock changes. In children, the brain starts to produce melatonin, the hormone that makes us sleepy, quite early in the evening. In teenagers, this happens about two hours later. So a fifteen-year-old who goes to bed at ten may simply not feel sleepy until midnight. But the school bus still leaves at seven forty-five.

Teenagers also need more sleep than adults — about eight to ten hours a night. If Ben falls asleep at midnight and gets up at seven, he sleeps only seven hours. Over a week, he loses many hours of sleep, and he tries to catch up at the weekend by sleeping until noon. Unfortunately, this moves his body clock even later, and Monday morning becomes even harder.

Some schools in different countries have tested a later start, for example at half past eight or nine instead of eight. The results were interesting: students slept longer, felt less sleepy in lessons, and in several studies their marks and attendance improved.

Ben's school didn't change its timetable, so his family tried other things. Ben agreed to leave his phone in the kitchen at ten. He started opening the curtains as soon as he woke up, because bright morning light helps to move the body clock earlier. At the weekend he got up no later than nine, even when he wanted to sleep more.
After a month, Ben still didn't love mornings. But his mother only needed to knock once.

p: Olga had prepared for the interview for a whole week. She had read everything about the company, practised answers to typical questions with her friend and chosen a smart dark blue jacket. The interview was at ten o'clock in an office on the fifth floor of a glass building in the city centre.

At nine fifteen she was already standing at the entrance. She didn't want to be too early, so she walked around the block twice. At a quarter to ten she went inside, but the lift wasn't working. She walked up five floors and arrived out of breath and a little red in the face.

There were three people on the interview panel: a woman from the personnel department, the head of the team and a young man who didn't say anything at first. The first questions were easy: Olga talked about her education and her last job. Then the head of the team asked her to describe a mistake she had made at work.

Olga hadn't prepared for this question. For a second she wanted to say something safe, like "I work too hard." But then she decided to tell the truth. She described how she had once sent a client the wrong price list, how she had noticed it the next morning, called the client herself and fixed the problem before it became serious. She also explained the system she now used to check documents before sending them.

At the end, the young man finally spoke. He asked her what she did when she disagreed with her manager. Olga answered that she preferred to discuss problems privately and to come with a possible solution, not only with a complaint.

Two days later she received a call. She had got the job. Later the head of the team told her why: many candidates had good education and experience, but Olga was the only one who had honestly talked about a mistake and what she had learned from it.

p: Last winter a big storm hit the small island where my grandparents live. The wind was so strong that it broke several electricity poles, and the whole island was left without power. The repair team could only come by boat, and the sea was too rough. So for three days, about two thousand people lived like their great-grandparents.

I was staying with my grandparents at the time. On the first evening, I panicked a little. My phone battery was at twenty percent, there was no internet, and the house was getting cold. My grandfather just smiled. He went to the shed and came back with an old oil lamp, a box of candles and a pile of dry wood for the fireplace.

We spent the evenings in one room, the only one we could keep warm. My grandmother cooked soup in a big pot on the wood stove. Without television or phones, we talked — really talked — for hours. My grandfather told stories about his years as a fisherman, including the night his boat was almost lost in a storm much worse than this one. I had never heard these stories before.

During the day, the island felt different too. Neighbours knocked on each other's doors to check that everyone was all right. A man who had a petrol generator invited people to charge their phones at his house. The small shop sold everything that could spoil quickly at half price, and a café gave away free hot tea.

On the third evening, the lights suddenly came back on. Everybody in the street cheered. The fridge started humming, the television came back to life, and my phone began to vibrate with dozens of messages.

I was happy, of course. But I was also a little sad. In those three days I had learned more about my family and my grandparents' neighbours than in all my previous visits together. Now, when I visit them, we sometimes turn off the lights for an evening, light the old lamp and just talk.

p: The building where Leo lives is grey, tall and ugly. For years its flat roof was covered with old chairs, broken boxes and pigeons. Nobody went up there except the man who repaired the television aerials once a year.

Then, one spring, a retired gardener named Mrs Patel moved into the flat on the top floor. A week later she asked the building manager if she could use the roof. He shrugged and said, "As long as it doesn't fall down." She took that as a yes.

She started with six wooden boxes filled with soil. In them she planted tomatoes, beans and some herbs. Leo, who was fourteen and bored that summer, watched her from the stairs. One day she handed him a watering can without saying a word, and he somehow found himself watering beans.

Over the summer, more neighbours came. A young couple brought strawberry plants. A man from the second floor, who had never spoken to anyone, built a simple bench from old wood. Two little girls painted the boxes in bright colours. People who had lived in the same building for years without knowing each other's names now argued happily about the best way to grow peppers.

Mrs Patel taught Leo a lot. She showed him how to tell if a plant needed water by touching the soil, why bees were important, and how to save seeds for the next year. But the most important lesson, he says, was about patience. "You can't pull a plant to make it grow faster," she told him. "You can only give it what it needs and wait."

In September the residents had a small party on the roof. They ate salad made from their own tomatoes and watched the sunset over the city. The building was still grey and tall, but it didn't feel ugly any more.
Now Leo is the one who hands the watering can to the new kids.

t: The Myth of the Productive Morning
p: Scroll through social media for long enough and you will find them: articles and videos promising that successful people wake up at five in the morning, meditate, journal, exercise, read and finish their most important work before most of us have had breakfast. The message is clear. If you want to achieve something, you need to become a morning person.

It is an attractive idea, mainly because it offers a simple recipe. Unfortunately, the evidence behind it is weaker than the confident tone suggests. Researchers who study sleep and daily rhythms agree on one thing above all: people differ. Our natural preferences for early or late hours, known as chronotypes, are partly genetic and change with age. Forcing a natural night owl to get up at five does not magically give them the energy of a lark. More often, it simply makes them tired.

What the early-rising stories usually leave out is the evening. People who get up at five and feel great typically go to bed at nine or ten. The benefit, if there is one, often comes from consistent sleep and quiet, uninterrupted time, not from the hour on the clock itself.

That second ingredient — uninterrupted time — may be the real secret. Many people feel productive early in the morning simply because nobody is sending them messages yet. The house is quiet, the inbox is still, and there are no meetings. In other words, what they are enjoying is not the morning but the absence of interruptions. A night owl who protects two quiet hours in the late evening may get exactly the same benefit.

Research on attention supports this. When we are interrupted, it can take a surprisingly long time to return fully to a complex task, and in the meantime we make more errors. Even expecting an interruption, such as keeping a phone face up on the desk, seems to reduce performance for some people. A protected block of focused time, whenever it happens, is valuable.

None of this means that routines are useless. A regular start to the day can reduce the number of decisions we have to make and help us begin work without negotiation. But the best routine is one that fits your body and your life, not someone else's.

So instead of copying a celebrity's schedule, it may be more useful to ask a few practical questions. When do I naturally feel most alert? When are the fewest people likely to need me? How much sleep do I actually need to feel well? The answers will be different for each of us.

There is one more advantage to this approach: it is sustainable. A routine that fights your biology tends to collapse after a few weeks, often leaving you feeling guilty. A routine built around your real rhythms can last for years. And in the long run, consistency matters far more than the time on the alarm clock.

If you happen to love early mornings, wonderful — enjoy the quiet sunrise. If you don't, you are not lazy or doomed to fail. You may simply need to find your own five o'clock, wherever it is on the clock.

p: On a clear day, from almost anywhere in the town where Marco grew up, you can see the mountain. It is beautiful: wide, green at the bottom and grey near the top, often wearing a small white cloud like a hat. It is also an active volcano. The last serious eruption happened more than seventy years ago, but scientists are quite sure there will be another one. The only question is when.

People who have never lived near a volcano often ask why anyone would choose to. The first answer is simple: the land. Volcanic soil, rich in minerals, is extraordinarily fertile. On the slopes around Marco's town, families have grown grapes, olives and lemons for centuries. His grandfather used to say that the mountain takes from you once in a lifetime, but feeds you every single day.

The second answer is history. Many families have lived in the same villages for generations. Their houses, churches and graveyards are there. Leaving would mean breaking a connection that feels more important than an abstract risk.

And for most people, the risk does feel abstract. Psychologists who study how we perceive danger have found that we tend to underestimate threats that are rare, slow and invisible, even when they could be severe. A car accident on a familiar road feels real; an eruption that might happen in twenty or two hundred years does not. The mountain is simply part of the landscape, like the sea or the sky.

Yet the volcano is watched very carefully. A network of instruments surrounds it: seismometers record even the smallest earthquakes, satellites measure tiny changes in the shape of the ground, and special sensors analyse the gases coming out of cracks near the top. Before an eruption, magma moving underground usually produces warning signs — more frequent small earthquakes, swelling of the ground, changes in the gases. Scientists cannot predict the exact day, but they can often see that something is changing weeks or months in advance.

That is why the town has an evacuation plan. Every few years there is a practice: sirens sound, schools close, and residents follow marked routes out of the danger zone. Marco remembers these days from his childhood as a strange mix of excitement and boredom — hours of waiting in buses on the main road while officials counted people.

The biggest challenge, according to the local civil protection office, is not the technology but trust. If scientists raise the alarm and the eruption does not come, people may ignore the next warning. If they wait too long to be completely sure, it may be too late. Communicating uncertainty honestly — "the danger is increasing, but we do not know exactly when" — is one of the hardest parts of the job.

There is also an economic side to the danger. Insurance for houses on the slopes is expensive, and some families cannot afford it. Local authorities have offered money to people who agree to move away from the most dangerous zone, but only a small number have accepted. For many, a payment cannot replace a place.

Marco now lives in a big city in the north. When he visits his parents, he still looks up at the mountain as soon as he gets off the train. He knows it is dangerous. But to him it also looks like home.

t: Why Small Kindness Feels Bigger Than We Expect
p: Imagine you are walking to work and see a colleague who looks stressed. You think about buying them a coffee, but then you hesitate. It's such a small thing. They probably won't care. It might even be awkward. So you walk past.
If this sounds familiar, you are not alone — and according to a growing body of research, you are probably wrong about how your gesture would have been received.

In a series of experiments published in 2022, psychologists asked participants to perform small acts of kindness, such as giving a cup of hot chocolate to a stranger in a park or writing a friendly note to a friend. Before doing so, participants predicted how the recipient would feel. Afterwards, the recipients themselves reported their actual feelings. The result was consistent: people systematically underestimated how positive the recipients would feel. The gesture that seemed trivial to the giver felt meaningful to the receiver.

Why does this gap exist? One explanation is that givers and receivers focus on different things. The person giving tends to think about the object itself — a coffee is just a coffee. The person receiving, however, pays more attention to the warmth behind it: someone noticed me, someone thought about me. That emotional message is far more powerful than the price of the gift.

A related set of studies looked at gratitude letters. Participants wrote short letters to people who had helped them in the past and predicted how surprised and pleased the recipients would be, and how awkward they would feel. Again, writers overestimated the awkwardness and underestimated the joy. Many recipients described the letters as deeply moving.

These misjudgements matter because they can stop us from acting. If we expect our kindness to have little impact, or to cause embarrassment, we are less likely to do it. Over time, this creates a world with fewer friendly gestures than people actually want — not because they are selfish, but because they misjudge the value of what they could give.

There is also a benefit for the giver. Numerous studies suggest that spending money or time on others tends to increase our own sense of happiness, sometimes more than spending the same amount on ourselves. In one well-known experiment, people who were given a small sum of money and told to spend it on someone else reported feeling happier at the end of the day than those who spent it on themselves.

None of this means that kindness should be calculated as a tool for personal happiness. But it does suggest a simple rule of thumb. When you notice an impulse to do something kind and hear the voice that says "it's too small to matter", remember the research. The other person will very likely appreciate it more than you think.

Researchers also point out that kindness spreads. In studies of groups, people who received help were more likely to help someone else afterwards, even a different person. One small gesture can start a chain that the original giver never sees.
So next time you see that stressed colleague, buy the coffee. It may be the best thing that happens to them that morning — and possibly to you as well.

t: The Last Customer of the Night Library
p: The city library had been open until midnight for only three months when Hannah, who worked the late shift, began to notice the man in the green coat.

He arrived every evening at exactly ten o'clock, chose the same table by the window on the second floor and stayed until the lights flickered as a sign that the library was closing. He never borrowed anything. He read newspapers, then a thick book about the history of bridges, then, as the evening went on, he simply sat and looked out at the river. He was perhaps seventy, always clean-shaven, with a small scar above his left eyebrow.

At first Hannah assumed he was homeless and came for the warmth. But his coat was expensive, if old, and once she saw him get into a taxi. Then she wondered if he was lonely, which seemed more likely. He never spoke to anyone except to say "Good evening" and "Thank you" in a quiet, careful voice with a slight accent she could not identify.

One night in February a heavy snowstorm closed most of the city's roads. By eleven the library was empty — except for the man in the green coat. When Hannah went upstairs to tell him that the buses had stopped, she found him standing at the window, looking at the snow falling on the river.
"I'm sorry," she said. "You might have trouble getting home tonight."

He turned and smiled. "I know. I've had trouble getting home for forty years." Seeing her confused face, he laughed softly and pointed at the old iron bridge below them. "I helped to build that bridge when I was a young engineer, newly arrived in this country. My wife and I used to walk across it every evening. She used to say it was the only place in the city where she felt she was neither here nor there, just in between."

His wife had died the previous autumn, he explained. Their flat was full of her things, and in the evenings it was unbearably quiet. When the library started opening late, he discovered that this table had the best view of the bridge in the whole city. "Here I am not alone," he said, "but nobody expects me to talk."

Hannah did not know what to say, so she said something practical. She called the night taxi service, which was still running, and waited with him downstairs. While they waited, he told her how the bridge had been built: the frozen winter when work had stopped for weeks, the accident that had left him with the scar above his eyebrow, the day it opened and his wife had walked across it first.

When the taxi finally came, he thanked her twice, which for him was almost a speech. Hannah watched the car disappear slowly into the snow and realised that she had worked in the library for two years without ever asking a single visitor about their life.
The next evening, he arrived at ten as usual. On his table Hannah had left a small card. On it she had written: "Reserved for the bridge engineer."
He did not mention it, but from that night on he said a little more than "Good evening".

p: For many people, putting a plastic bottle into the recycling bin is a small, satisfying act. It feels like the problem has been solved: the bottle will be collected, cleaned, melted and turned into something new. Unfortunately, the reality is more complicated, and understanding it can help us make better choices.

The first problem is that "plastic" is not one material but a family of very different ones. Bottles for water and soft drinks are usually made of a type called PET, which is relatively easy to recycle. Milk containers are often made of another type, HDPE, which is also commonly recycled. But many other items — yoghurt pots, food trays, films and bags, toys, packaging made of several layers stuck together — are much harder or impossible to process with the machines most recycling plants have.

The second problem is contamination. A container with food left inside, a greasy pizza box or a bottle with the wrong kind of cap can reduce the quality of a whole batch of material. Recycling plants have to sort enormous quantities quickly, and items that cannot be identified or cleaned easily are often sent to landfill or burned.

The third problem is economics. Recycled plastic has to compete with new plastic made from oil, which is often cheaper. When oil prices are low, there is little financial reason for manufacturers to choose recycled material. For many years, some wealthy countries also exported large amounts of plastic waste to other parts of the world, where it was not always processed safely. When several of those countries restricted imports, it became clear how much of the "recycled" plastic had never really been recycled at all.

Finally, plastic cannot be recycled endlessly. Each time it is melted and reprocessed, the long chains of molecules that give it strength become shorter, and the material becomes weaker. A bottle may become a fleece jacket or a carpet, but these products are rarely recycled again. In practice, much recycling is better described as "downcycling".

There is even a psychological trap. Some studies suggest that when people know an item can be recycled, they use more of it, as if the recycling bin cancelled out the waste. In one experiment, participants used noticeably more paper towels when a recycling bin was placed next to them. The feeling of doing the right thing can make us less careful.

Does this mean recycling is pointless? Not at all. Recycling the right materials correctly still saves energy and resources. Clean PET bottles, aluminium cans and paper are worth putting in the bin. But it does mean that recycling should be seen as the last option rather than the first.

Environmental organisations often summarise this with three words in a particular order: reduce, reuse, recycle. The most effective step is to avoid unnecessary plastic in the first place — carrying a reusable bottle, choosing products with less packaging, refusing items we don't really need. The next best is to use things many times. Recycling comes third, after the first two options have been tried.
So next time you drop a bottle into the bin, it is worth asking a slightly uncomfortable question: could I have avoided this bottle altogether?

t: How Bees Decide Where to Live
p: Every spring, in thousands of gardens and forests, a remarkable decision is made without a leader, a vote count or a single word. A colony of honeybees that has grown too large splits in two. The old queen leaves with about half of the workers — often more than ten thousand bees — and the swarm must find a new home within a few days. If it chooses badly, the colony may not survive the winter.

The swarm first gathers in a temporary cluster, typically hanging from a tree branch like a large, buzzing beard. From there, a few hundred experienced bees, known as scouts, fly out to search the surrounding area. They are looking for a cavity with very particular qualities: a volume of roughly forty litres, a small entrance facing south, a position several metres above the ground and dry walls. A hollow tree is ideal.

When a scout finds a promising site, she inspects it carefully, sometimes for many minutes, walking around inside to measure it. Then she returns to the cluster and performs a waggle dance on its surface. The direction of the dance tells other bees which way to fly, and the duration of the waggle indicates the distance. Crucially, the enthusiasm of the dance depends on the quality of the site: a scout who has found an excellent cavity dances many more circuits than one who has found a mediocre place.

Other scouts who watch the dance may fly out to inspect the site themselves. If they like it, they return and dance for it too. In this way, good sites recruit more and more supporters, while poor sites gradually lose their dancers. Interestingly, each scout's enthusiasm fades with every return trip, so even supporters of a good site eventually stop dancing. This prevents early discoveries from dominating simply because they were found first.

The decision is reached when enough scouts — about twenty or thirty — are gathered at one site at the same time. This is called a quorum. When the scouts at that site sense the quorum, they fly back and make a special piping sound that tells the whole swarm to warm up its flight muscles. Within an hour, thousands of bees rise into the air and fly together to their new home.

The biologist Thomas Seeley, who studied this process for decades, tested how good these decisions really are. On an island with no natural cavities, he offered swarms a choice of wooden nest boxes of different quality. In most cases, the swarms chose the best box, even when it was not the first one discovered.

What the swarm avoids is just as interesting. No single bee compares all the options; most scouts visit only one or two sites. There is no discussion in which the most confident individual persuades the rest. The quality of the decision emerges from many independent judgements combined by a simple rule.

Seeley argues that human groups could learn from bees. A good decision process, in his view, includes a diverse search of options, open debate, independent evaluation of each option and a clear rule for when to stop discussing. Groups that rely on a single leader or rush to agree on the first idea often do worse.

t: The Attention Economy and the Art of Not Looking
p: In 1971, long before smartphones existed, the economist and psychologist Herbert Simon made an observation that now sounds prophetic. In a world rich in information, he wrote, what information consumes is the attention of its recipients. A wealth of information creates a poverty of attention. Half a century later, that sentence reads less like a theory and more like a description of an ordinary afternoon.

The basic logic is simple. Many of the digital services we use every day are free at the point of use. They are paid for by advertising, and advertising is sold by the quantity and quality of attention delivered to it. The longer we stay, the more we scroll, the more valuable we become. This has given rise to what is often called the attention economy: a vast industry whose central product is not software or content, but time spent looking at a screen.

Designers in this industry are not villains, and most of them are simply trying to make products people enjoy. But the incentives push in a particular direction. Features that increase engagement tend to survive; features that help users leave tend to disappear. Infinite scroll removes the natural stopping point that the bottom of a page used to provide. Autoplay starts the next video before we have decided whether we want it. Notifications arrive at irregular intervals, which, as decades of behavioural research suggest, is one of the most effective ways to keep someone checking.

There is a temptation to describe all of this in the language of addiction, and some researchers do. Others are more cautious, pointing out that heavy use is not necessarily harmful and that studies linking screen time to wellbeing often find only small effects. What seems clearer is a quieter cost: fragmentation. When attention is constantly interrupted, deep work, sustained reading and long conversations become harder, not because we lack intelligence but because we rarely give our minds the uninterrupted time those activities require.

The philosopher and writer who worries about this most is not necessarily the one who throws away their phone. Complete abstinence is rarely realistic, and it can turn into a kind of moral performance. A more interesting approach is to treat attention as something that can be designed, just as the products competing for it are designed.

That might begin with the environment. Moving a distracting app off the home screen, switching the screen to grey tones, or charging the phone outside the bedroom introduces small amounts of friction. Behavioural scientists have repeatedly found that minor obstacles — a few extra taps, a few metres of distance — can significantly reduce impulsive behaviour, precisely because so much of our checking is not a decision at all, but a reflex.

It might continue with time. Instead of trying to resist distractions all day, which is exhausting, some people schedule specific periods for messages and news, and protect other periods completely. This approach, sometimes called time-blocking, shifts the question from "Can I resist?" to "Is this the time for it?" — a far easier question to answer.

And it might extend to a deeper question about what we want our attention to serve. Attention is not just a resource; in a real sense, it is what our lives are made of. The things we repeatedly attend to shape what we notice, what we care about and, eventually, who we become. The psychologist William James made a similar point more than a century ago when he suggested that our experience is, to a large extent, what we agree to attend to.

Seen this way, the most radical act in the attention economy may not be outrage or withdrawal, but a deliberate kind of looking: choosing, again and again, where the light of attention falls. It requires no special equipment, only practice — the patient habit of noticing when our attention has been taken, and gently taking it back.

It is worth adding that the same tools that fragment attention can also protect it. Many phones now offer focus modes, screen-time reports and scheduled silence. These features will not solve the problem on their own, but they show that design can work in either direction, depending on what users ask for.

None of this is easy, and nobody manages it perfectly. But just as a city can be planned for cars or for people, a day can be planned for distraction or for focus. The technology will keep evolving. The question of what we look at, and why, remains ours.

t: The Map Is Not the Territory
p: In the eighteenth century, cartographers who did not know what lay inside a continent faced an awkward choice. They could leave the interior blank and admit their ignorance, or they could fill it with something. Many chose the second option. They drew mountains where travellers had heard rumours of mountains, rivers that might or might not exist, and occasionally an elephant or two to cover an inconvenient empty space. For decades, maps of West Africa included a long range called the Mountains of Kong, which explorers reported, copied and repeated until, late in the nineteenth century, someone finally went to look and found that they simply were not there.

The story is amusing, but it illustrates a principle that reaches far beyond geography. In the 1930s the philosopher Alfred Korzybski summarised it in a phrase that has since become famous: the map is not the territory. Every representation of reality — a map, a model, a theory, a set of statistics, a mental picture of another person — is a simplification. It leaves things out, and it may contain things that are not really there.

This is not a flaw that better maps could eliminate. It is the whole point of a map. A map at a scale of one to one, showing every stone and blade of grass, would be as large as the land itself and therefore useless. Simplification is what makes representations helpful. The danger begins when we forget that we are looking at a simplification and start treating the map as if it were the world.

Examples are everywhere. A company may become so focused on a measurable target — the number of calls answered per hour, for instance — that employees learn to end calls quickly instead of solving customers' problems. The economist Charles Goodhart gave his name to a version of this observation: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. The number was a useful map of good service until people began steering by the number itself.

Something similar happens in our personal lives. We carry mental maps of the people around us: my colleague is lazy, my brother is irresponsible, I am bad at mathematics. These labels save effort, but they can also prevent us from noticing evidence that contradicts them. A colleague who stays late every evening to support a sick parent may still be filed under "lazy" because she leaves meetings early. The map has stopped being updated.

Scientists have developed habits to guard against this. A good scientific model comes with an explicit statement of its assumptions and limits. Researchers are trained, at least in principle, to look for observations that could prove them wrong rather than ones that confirm what they already believe. When the facts and the model disagree, the model is supposed to change. In practice, of course, scientists are human and often defend their maps longer than they should, but the ideal remains valuable.

History offers more dramatic cases. Generals have lost battles because their maps showed roads that had been washed away, and economists have failed to foresee crises because their models assumed that markets always behave rationally. In each case, the problem was not the existence of a model, but the confidence placed in it after the world had quietly changed.

For the rest of us, a few simple questions can help. What has this picture left out? Who made it, and for what purpose? When was it last checked against reality? What would I expect to see if it were wrong? Asking them does not mean rejecting maps — we could not function without them — but holding them a little more loosely.

There is also a certain freedom in this way of thinking. If my belief that I am bad at mathematics is a map rather than a fact, then it can be redrawn. Perhaps it was drawn by a single unkind teacher, or by one bad exam at the age of twelve. Perhaps the territory — my actual ability, which grows with practice — looks quite different from the old map I have been carrying around.

The explorers who finally walked through the region where the Mountains of Kong were supposed to be did not find disappointment. They found the real landscape, which was more interesting than the imaginary one. That may be the best reason of all to keep checking our maps: reality, when we finally look at it, is usually richer than our picture of it.

p: Few emotions have as bad a reputation as boredom. We treat it as a problem to be solved immediately, preferably with a screen. Waiting rooms have televisions, queues have phones, and children on long car journeys are handed tablets before the first motorway exit. It has become entirely possible to go weeks without being bored for more than a few seconds at a time. Yet a growing number of psychologists argue that in eliminating boredom so efficiently, we may have lost something valuable.

To understand why, it helps to know what boredom actually is. Researchers usually define it as the uncomfortable feeling of wanting to be engaged in satisfying activity while being unable to engage. It is not the same as having nothing to do; you can be bored in the middle of a busy meeting. It is better described as a mismatch between the attention we have available and the things around us that could absorb it.

Seen in this light, boredom is less like a malfunction and more like a signal. Just as hunger tells us to eat and pain tells us to protect an injured part of the body, boredom tells us that what we are doing is not meeting our needs. Its unpleasantness is the point: it pushes us to look for something else — a new goal, a different approach, a more meaningful activity.

Some intriguing studies suggest that boredom can also make us more creative. In one frequently cited experiment, participants first performed a deliberately dull task, such as copying numbers from a telephone directory, and were then asked to think of as many uses as possible for a pair of plastic cups. Those who had been bored first produced more ideas, on average, than those who had not. The researchers proposed that the restless mind, searching for stimulation, begins to wander, and that wandering can lead to unexpected connections.

Mind wandering itself has been studied extensively. When we are not focused on a task, a network of brain regions sometimes called the default mode network becomes more active. This network seems to be involved in remembering the past, imagining the future, thinking about other people and constructing our sense of self. It is, in other words, busy precisely when we appear to be doing nothing.

It would be wrong to romanticise boredom entirely. Chronic boredom — a persistent sense that life lacks meaning and stimulation — is associated with poorer mental health, risky behaviour and, in some studies, overeating and substance use. A teenager in a town with no activities and no prospects is not experiencing a creative opportunity; they are experiencing a problem that society should address. The argument is not that boredom is good in itself, but that short, ordinary episodes of it can be useful if we allow them to run their course.

The difficulty is that we rarely do. Reaching for a phone the moment boredom appears is so easy that the signal never has a chance to work. Instead of asking ourselves what we actually want to do, we cover the discomfort with a stream of small stimulations, none of which really satisfies the need that boredom was pointing to. Afterwards, we often feel strangely empty — a sensation that some researchers describe as a kind of "boredom hangover".

What might a healthier relationship with boredom look like? It could be as simple as occasionally leaving the phone in a pocket while waiting for a bus, letting the mind drift for a few minutes. It could mean allowing children some unstructured time instead of filling every hour with organised activities. It could mean noticing the feeling of boredom at work and asking whether it signals that a task needs to be redesigned, delegated or simply finished more quickly.

Interestingly, people differ in how easily they become bored. Some researchers measure a trait called boredom proneness, and those who score high on it often report difficulty paying attention in general. For them, simply waiting out boredom may be harder, and learning to direct attention deliberately may matter even more.

Many writers and scientists have described their best ideas arriving in moments of apparent idleness: on walks, in the shower, while staring out of a train window. These stories should be treated with some caution, since we tend to remember the times an idea came and forget the many times nothing happened. But they point to a real possibility. Sometimes the most productive thing we can do is to stop filling every gap and see what our own mind offers when it is left alone for a while.

p: For twenty-two years, Irina Volkova had been the voice of other people. At international conferences she sat in a glass booth at the back of the hall, headphones pressed to her ears, and turned a stream of English into Russian almost as fast as it was spoken. Delegates rarely looked at the booth. If she did her job well, they forgot she existed. The best compliment an interpreter could receive, her first teacher had told her, was to be invisible.

She was good at being invisible. She could follow a nervous minister through a badly written speech, rescue a joke that did not work in translation, and keep her voice calm when a speaker shouted. Between sessions she drank tea from a thermos, reviewed glossaries of technical terms and spoke very little. Colleagues admired her concentration; a few found her cold.

The conference that changed things was a small one, held in a cold northern city in early spring. The subject was river pollution, and the speakers were engineers, biologists and representatives of villages along a river that ran through three countries. On the second afternoon an elderly woman from one of those villages came to the microphone. She had not been on the programme. Someone had given her five minutes.

She spoke in English, slowly, with a strong accent and many pauses. She did not use any statistics. She talked about her grandmother, who had washed clothes in the river, about the fish her father used to catch, about the summer when the water first turned a strange colour and the children were told not to swim. She said that she had come because nobody in her village knew what the scientific words in the reports meant, and they wanted someone to tell them, simply, whether the river would recover.

Irina had interpreted thousands of speeches more important than this one. But as she listened, she found that her usual technique — staying two or three words behind the speaker, never letting emotion into her voice — was not working. The woman's sentences were simple, and their simplicity was the problem. There was nothing technical to hide behind. To translate "the children were told not to swim" in the neutral, professional tone she had used for twenty-two years suddenly seemed like a small lie.

She made a decision she would later struggle to explain. She let her voice change. Not dramatically — no interpreter would ever imitate tears — but she allowed the pauses to stay where the woman had put them, and she did not smooth out the hesitations. When the woman said that she was tired of being polite, Irina said it, in Russian, as if she were tired too.

When the session ended, an engineer from the Russian-speaking delegation walked to the back of the hall and knocked on the glass booth. Irina took off her headphones, expecting a complaint. Instead, he asked who had written the speech. She explained that nobody had written it; the woman had simply spoken. He looked at her for a moment and then said that it was the first thing he had understood properly in two days.

That evening, for the first time in many years, Irina joined her colleagues for dinner instead of returning to her hotel room. They talked about the profession, as interpreters always do, and someone repeated the old rule about invisibility. Irina surprised herself by disagreeing. Invisibility, she said, was right for most speeches. But perhaps the real rule was faithfulness — to the meaning, and sometimes to the feeling. If a speech was cold, it should be cold in translation. If it was not, then perhaps the interpreter had no right to make it so.

Her colleagues argued with her, and the argument went on long after dessert. Some said that once interpreters started deciding which emotions to transmit, they would become actors, and nobody would be able to trust them. Others admitted that they had faced the same dilemma and had never known what to do.

Irina did not resolve the question that night, and she never fully resolved it afterwards. She went on working in the glass booth for another eight years, and for most of that time she was as invisible as ever. But she kept a small note in the cover of her glossary, written in pencil, that she looked at before difficult sessions. It said, in English: "Not a machine. A bridge."

t: The Strange Economics of Free Time
p: In 1930, in the middle of an economic depression, the British economist John Maynard Keynes wrote a short essay with a surprisingly optimistic title: "Economic Possibilities for Our Grandchildren". Looking a century ahead, he predicted that productivity would grow so much that people in rich countries would need to work only about fifteen hours a week. The great challenge of the future, he suggested, would not be scarcity but leisure — how to use all that free time wisely.

On the first part, Keynes was remarkably accurate. Productivity in developed economies has increased roughly as much as he expected; we produce far more per hour of work than people did in 1930. On the second part, he was spectacularly wrong. Average working hours have fallen since then, but nowhere near fifteen. Many professionals, in fact, report working longer hours than their parents did. What happened?

Economists offer several explanations, and they are not mutually exclusive. The first is that our desires grew along with our income. Keynes imagined that once basic needs were met, people would be satisfied. Instead, new products, services and experiences keep appearing, and what once seemed a luxury — a car, foreign holidays, a smartphone — quickly becomes a normal expectation. We chose, collectively, to turn much of our extra productivity into more consumption rather than more free time.

The second explanation concerns status. Many goods matter to us not only for what they do, but for what they say about our position relative to others. If everyone's income rises, the race for a larger house in a better neighbourhood does not end; it simply moves to a higher level. The economist Fred Hirsch called such goods "positional", and he argued that competition for them can keep people working hard even when, in absolute terms, they already have plenty.

The third explanation is that work itself changed. For many people, particularly in skilled professions, work is no longer only a source of income but also of identity, social contact and meaning. Being busy has even become a kind of status symbol. Studies in several countries have found that people sometimes describe themselves as overworked partly to signal that they are important and in demand.

The fourth explanation is structural. Employers often find it cheaper to have fewer employees working long hours than more employees working short ones, because each worker brings fixed costs such as training, equipment and benefits. In some jobs, being present for long hours is taken as a sign of commitment, regardless of how productive those hours are.

Yet there is a paradox here. Research on wellbeing consistently suggests that, beyond a certain level of income, additional money produces relatively small gains in happiness, while time spent with friends and family, in nature or on absorbing activities matters a great deal. Some studies have found that people who prioritise time over money report greater life satisfaction, even after accounting for income. If that is true, many of us may be making a poor trade.

Interestingly, when people do receive more free time, they do not always use it well. Surveys of how people spend their leisure hours show that a large share goes to passive activities such as watching screens, which people themselves often rate as less satisfying than more active pursuits. Keynes, it turns out, may have been right that leisure would be a challenge — just not in the way he imagined.

Several companies and governments have experimented with shorter working weeks, typically four days instead of five, without reducing pay. Results from these trials are encouraging but not yet conclusive. Many participating firms reported that productivity stayed roughly the same, while employees described less stress and better sleep. Critics point out that the companies that volunteered for such trials may not be typical, and that some kinds of work, such as caring for patients, cannot easily be compressed.
There is a historical irony here too. The two-day weekend itself was once a radical experiment that many employers believed would ruin their businesses.

Whatever the future of the working week, Keynes's question remains surprisingly relevant at the level of the individual. Even without a fifteen-hour week, most of us have some choice about how to trade money, status and time. Asking honestly what we are working for — and whether the extra hour is buying something we truly value — may be one of the most practical economic questions we can ask.

p: Walk into an old forest after a long walk through farmland and you may notice a change before you can name it. The air is cooler and damper. Sounds are softer. The ground gives slightly under your feet, as if you were walking on a sponge. What you are sensing is, in part, history: the slow accumulation of centuries of life and death that a young plantation, however green, has not yet had time to build.

Ecologists distinguish between old-growth forests, which have developed over long periods with relatively little human disturbance, and younger or managed forests. From a distance they may look similar. Up close, the differences are striking. Old forests contain trees of many different ages and sizes, from seedlings to giants several centuries old. They contain standing dead trees and fallen trunks in every stage of decay. And they have deep, complex soils rich in organic matter.

That dead wood, which a tidy-minded forester might once have removed, turns out to be essential. A fallen tree becomes a home and a food source for an astonishing number of organisms: fungi, beetles, mosses, salamanders, birds that nest in cavities. In some European forests, a significant proportion of all species depend on dead or dying wood at some point in their lives. As the trunk slowly rots, it releases nutrients back into the soil and holds water like a reservoir during dry periods. A forest without dead wood is, in an important sense, a forest with a broken memory.

The soil itself holds another kind of memory. Beneath the surface, the roots of most trees form partnerships with fungi. The fine threads of the fungi, far thinner than roots, extend through the soil and help trees absorb water and minerals; in return, the trees supply the fungi with sugars produced by photosynthesis. These networks can be enormous. Some researchers have suggested that they may also connect neighbouring trees and allow resources to move between them, an idea that became popular under the name "wood wide web". The extent and importance of such sharing is still debated, and some scientists warn that popular accounts have gone far beyond the evidence. What is not disputed is that healthy forest soils are full of living connections that take a long time to develop.

These features help explain why old forests are so valuable for storing carbon. Large old trees continue to absorb carbon dioxide for many decades, and the deep soils and fallen wood hold even more. When an old forest is cut down, much of this stored carbon returns to the atmosphere, and it can take a century or more for a new forest to recover it — if it is allowed to grow that long.

Planting new trees is therefore useful, but it is not the same as protecting old ones. A newly planted forest of a single species, all of the same age, offers far fewer habitats than a mature mixed forest and is often more vulnerable to pests, storms and fire. Some scientists compare it to replacing an ancient library with a shelf of new books by one author: better than an empty room, but not a substitute for what was lost.

Old forests also carry human memory. In many regions, ancient woodlands contain traces of past use — boundary banks, charcoal-burning platforms, paths worn by generations of feet. Specific plants, such as certain spring flowers that spread only very slowly, can indicate that a patch of woodland has existed continuously for hundreds of years. Ecologists sometimes use these species as clues when mapping which forests are truly old.

What can an ordinary person do with this knowledge? Supporting the protection of existing old forests is often more effective than funding new plantations. In gardens and parks, leaving a pile of logs or a dead branch in place can provide a small refuge for insects and fungi. And when walking in an old forest, it is worth slowing down and noticing what has taken centuries to build: the mossy trunk, the soft ground, the cool, still air.

The forest does not remember in the way a person does. But it accumulates the results of its past in its structure, its soil and its inhabitants. Once lost, that accumulation cannot be quickly replaced. In an age that values speed, old forests are a rare reminder that some kinds of wealth can only be grown slowly.
